blocks.prompt: 11 (i) Find the values of \(u\) and \(v\) if \((u + iv)^2 = 20 + 21i\).
blocks.explanation:
Same idea as Question 3, with letters \(u, v\) instead of \(x, y\).
We must find \(u\) and \(v\) (two pairs).
Plan: compare parts, find \(u^2 + v^2\), add and subtract, fix the signs.
steps:
Given: \((u + iv)^2 = 20 + 21i\), \(u, v\) real.
To find: \(u\) and \(v\).
Method: Expand \((u + iv)^2\), compare parts, then use the identity \((u^2 + v^2)^2 = (u^2 - v^2)^2 + (2uv)^2\) to get \(u^2 + v^2\). Adding and subtracting gives \(u^2\) and \(v^2\); the sign of \(2uv\) decides which signs go together.

Compare real and imaginary parts
\[u^2 - v^2 = 20 \quad (1)\]
\[2uv = 21 \quad (2)\]
Why: Equality of complex numbers.

Find \(u^2 + v^2\)
\[(u^2 + v^2)^2 = (u^2 - v^2)^2 + (2uv)^2\]
\[= 20^2 + 21^2\]
\[= 400 + 441 = 841\]
\[u^2 + v^2 = 29 \quad (3)\]
Why: This identity is true for all numbers (expand both sides to see it). \(u^2 + v^2\) can never be negative, so we take the positive square root.

Add (1) and (3) to find \(u\)
\[2u^2 = 20 + 29 = 49\]
\[u^2 = \dfrac{49}{2}\]
\[u = \pm\dfrac{7}{\sqrt{2}} = \pm\dfrac{7\sqrt{2}}{2}\]
Why: Adding cancels \(v^2\). A square root always gives two signs, \(\pm\).

Subtract (1) from (3) to find \(v\)
\[2v^2 = 29 - 20 = 9\]
\[v^2 = \dfrac{9}{2}\]
\[v = \pm\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} = \pm\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\]
Why: Subtracting cancels \(u^2\).

Decide which signs go together
\[2uv = 21\]
\[u = \dfrac{7\sqrt{2}}{2},\ v = \dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\]
\[\text{or } u = -\dfrac{7\sqrt{2}}{2},\ v = -\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\]
Why: \(2uv\) is positive, so \(u\) and \(v\) have the same sign. Pairing them wrongly would square to the wrong imaginary part.

Check
\[u^2 - v^2 = \dfrac{49}{2} - \dfrac{9}{2} = 20 \;\checkmark\]
\[2uv = 2 \cdot \dfrac{7}{\sqrt{2}} \cdot \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\]
\[= 2 \cdot \dfrac{21}{2} = 21 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Both equations (1) and (2) are satisfied.

blocks.prompt: 11 (ii) Find the values of \(u\) and \(v\) if \((u + iv)^2 = 48 - 10i\).
blocks.explanation:
Same method as part (i); this time the numbers are not perfect squares, so the answer contains nested roots.
We must find \(u\) and \(v\).
Plan: compare parts, \(u^2 + v^2\), add and subtract; \(2uv\) is negative, so the signs are opposite.
steps:
Given: \((u + iv)^2 = 48 - 10i\), \(u, v\) real.
To find: \(u\) and \(v\).
Method: Expand \((u + iv)^2\), compare parts, then use the identity \((u^2 + v^2)^2 = (u^2 - v^2)^2 + (2uv)^2\) to get \(u^2 + v^2\). Adding and subtracting gives \(u^2\) and \(v^2\); the sign of \(2uv\) decides which signs go together.

Compare real and imaginary parts
\[u^2 - v^2 = 48 \quad (1)\]
\[2uv = -10 \quad (2)\]
Why: Equality of complex numbers.

Find \(u^2 + v^2\)
\[(u^2 + v^2)^2 = (u^2 - v^2)^2 + (2uv)^2\]
\[= 48^2 + (-10)^2\]
\[= 2304 + 100 = 2404\]
\[\sqrt{2404} = \sqrt{4 \times 601} = 2\sqrt{601}\]
\[u^2 + v^2 = 2\sqrt{601} \quad (3)\]
Why: This identity is true for all numbers (expand both sides to see it). \(u^2 + v^2\) can never be negative, so we take the positive square root.

Add (1) and (3) to find \(u\)
\[2u^2 = 48 + 2\sqrt{601}\]
\[u^2 = 24 + \sqrt{601}\]
\[u = \pm\sqrt{24 + \sqrt{601}}\]
Why: Adding cancels \(v^2\). A square root always gives two signs, \(\pm\).

Subtract (1) from (3) to find \(v\)
\[2v^2 = 2\sqrt{601} - 48\]
\[v^2 = \sqrt{601} - 24\]
\[v = \pm\sqrt{\sqrt{601} - 24}\]
Why: Subtracting cancels \(u^2\).

Decide which signs go together
\[2uv = -10\]
\[u = \sqrt{24 + \sqrt{601}}\]
\[v = -\sqrt{\sqrt{601} - 24}\]
\[\text{or the same with signs swapped}\]
\[u \approx \pm 6.97,\quad v \approx \mp 0.72\]
Why: \(2uv\) is negative, so \(u\) and \(v\) have opposite signs. Pairing them wrongly would square to the wrong imaginary part.

Check
\[u^2 - v^2 = (24 + \sqrt{601}) - (\sqrt{601} - 24)\]
\[= 48 \;\checkmark\]
\[uv = -\sqrt{(\sqrt{601} + 24)(\sqrt{601} - 24)}\]
\[= -\sqrt{601 - 576} = -5\]
\[2uv = -10 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Both equations (1) and (2) are satisfied.
